abstract: Objectives: Greater vulnerability of Black vs. White individuals to cardiovascular disease (CVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) is well charted in the United States, but studies involving sub-Saharan blacks are scarce. Methods: Baseline data (2021–2024) were collected in 168 sub-Saharan Blacks and 93 European Whites in an ongoing clinical trial ( NCT04299529 ), using standardized patient selection criteria. Data included clinical and biochemical risk factors, ECG and echocardiographic traits, Framingham CVD risk, CKD grades (KDIGO 2024), self-assessed symptoms (WHO questionnaire), and urinary proteomic profiles predictive of left ventricular dysfunction (LVD) and CKD, HF1, and CKD273, respectively. Racial comparisons rested on unadjusted and multivariable-adjusted analyses. Results: Despite being younger (60.4 vs. 68.3 years), blacks had a worse risk profile, as evidenced by higher diabetes prevalence, higher BMI, faster heart rate, unfavourable serum cholesterol fractions, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate, microalbuminuria, and sedentary lifestyle. This resulted in blacks having higher 10-year CVD risk, higher heart age (index of vascular ageing with chronological age as reference), and a worse CKD grades. In both races, CKD273 increased with CKD grade, but CKD273 and HF1 were not different by race. These observations were robust in subgroup and adjusted analyses. Conclusion: This study did not differentiate host (genetic, molecular, and pathogenic) from environmental drivers of disease. Nonetheless, the findings call for a multipronged and comprehensive implementation of innovative health policies in sub-Saharan countries. Education, research, empowerment of stakeholders, and international learned societies connecting experts from a wide array of disciplines should vigorously sustain this effort.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
UPRIGHT-HTM (Clinicaltrials.gov identifier:
NCT04299529
) complies with the Helsinki declaration [
18
]. The Ethics Committee of University Hospitals Leuven, Belgium (Belgian registration number, B3222020000276), acting as the central Ethics Committee and, the Institutional Review Boards of all clinical sites approved the trial protocol [
16
]. Patients provide written informed consent using paper forms translated in the native languages of the catchment areas. These forms are the only paper documents in the trial and allow identification of the patients. However, in line with the European General Data Protection Regulations [
19
], these forms have to be filed in each patient's local medical record [
16
] and are not part of the electronic trial data.
Design of UPRIGHT-HTM
UPRIGHT-HTM is an investigator-initiated randomized clinical trial, of which the rationale and protocol [
16
] and first progress report [
17
] are published. The UPP-associated risk is communicated to caregivers and patients early during follow-up in the intervention group and only after completion of follow-up in the control group. The underlying hypothesis is that refinement of risk assessment in the intervention group by UPP on top of HTM will motivate caregivers and patients to more stringent management of risk factors and therefore to a lower incidence of the primary endpoint, a composite of intermediate target organ damage, including CKD and diastolic LVD, and hard cardiovascular and renal events [
16
].
Active recruitment is currently ongoing in Europe (Belgium, Kosovo, Poland, and Slovenia), Asia (China), sub-Saharan Africa (Mozambique, Nigeria, and South-Africa), and South America (La Plata, Argentina). Eligible patients are asymptomatic adults of either sex and must in addition to being aged (55–75 years) have five or more guideline-defined risk factors, preferably including hypertension, type-2 diabetes mellitus, or both. Furthermore, to qualify, patients must have an e-mail address, internet access via an android smartphone, and be willing to engage in HTM during follow-up. Asymptomatic patients with CKD stage 3A [
20
] or diastolic LVD (stage-1 heart failure) meet the entry criteria on condition that only one of these two disorders is present. On top of the exclusion criteria common to all clinical trials, study-specific exclusion criteria comprise an impracticable echocardiographic window, atrial fibrillation or flutter or frequent extrasystoles, because these conditions interfere with the echocardiographic assessment of LVD and HTM using oscillometric devices [
16
]. After a screening visit and a run-in period of variable length (1–5 weeks or longer), patients are stratified by centre and sex and randomized using a fully automated web-based computerized random function [
16
].
Data collection
UPRIGHT-HTM is running as a patient-centred trial, mainly positioned at the patients’ homes and primary care practices or out-patient clinics, using the CE-certified web-based and highly secured WiPaM platform (
Wi
reless
Pa
tient
M
onitoring), developed by RDSM NV, Hasselt, Belgium (
https://www.rdsm.eu
). Data are collected electronically by patients using the android-based app and by their caregivers via electronic case report forms (eCRFs). Data collection is described in detail in the online only Supplemental Material.
Mosaiques-Diagnostics GmbH, Hannover, Germany (MOS) did the UPP profiling for all patients. HF1 and CKD273 are validated urinary proteomic markers of imminent diastolic LVD and CKD. HF1 and CKD273 are expressed in normalized units and are normally distributed. The thresholds indicating increased risk are at least -0.350 for HF1 and more than 0.154 for CKD273 (Supplemental Material, pages 5–6).
Statistical analysis
The current analysis is restricted to baseline data collected at the screening and prerandomization visits. For data management and statistical analysis, SAS software, version 9.4, maintenance level 5 (SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina, USA) is used. As defined in the trial protocol [
16
], an intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analysis was conducted. Deviation from the normal distribution was assessed by the Shapiro-Wilk statistic. The central tendency (spread) of variables is represented by the arithmetic mean (SD) for normally distributed variables and by the median (interquartile range [IQR]) for nonnormally distributed continuous variables. Categorical variables are presented as proportions.
For the current analysis, group means and medians were compared by the unpaired
t
-test and the Mann–Whitney
U
test, respectively, while proportions were compared by a χ2-statistic or Fisher exact test, as appropriate according to the cell counts. Pearson or rank correlation coefficients, as appropriate given the distributional characteristics of the variables of interest, were computed and compared between races, using Fisher Z transform [
21
]. Statistical methods also included multiple linear regression (general linear model) and logistic regression for modelling binary of ordinal outcomes in relation to covariables. Statistical significance is a two-sided α-level of 0.05.
Risk of CVD and heart age were derived from the sex-specific Framingham risk score (FRS) derived from age, total serum cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, SBP, antihypertensive treatment status (yes vs. no), smoking (yes vs. no), and diabetes (yes vs. no) [
22
]. Heart age reflects the biological vascular age [
22
]. CKD grades are categorized by cross-classification of eGFR and albuminuria according the 2024 KDIGO Guideline [
20
]. The traditional risk factors, cardiac function by echocardiography, and the risk of CVD and CKD grades were contrasted between sub-Saharan Blacks and European Whites. Age was categorized using ordinal 5-year groups ranging from less than 55 to at least 70 years.

INTRODUCTION
Sub-Saharan countries face persisting health challenges, such as infectious diseases, malnutrition, and child and maternal mortality, and more recently the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) [
1
,
2
]. A major cause is the demographic revolution, characterized by longer life expectancy, but also by lengthier disability-adjusted life-years and lower quality of life [
3
]. Hypertension, obesity, and type-2 diabetes are the drivers of the NCD burden sub-Saharan Africa [
4
,
5
], where population health indicators generally remain behind most other low-income and middle-income countries [
2
,
6
]. Climate change [
1
], the degradation of the living environment, overcrowded metropolitan areas [
1
], and changing eating habits with surplus amounts of sugar and processed foods [
6
] increasingly contribute to the sub-Saharan NCD burden.
The racial disparity between blacks and whites in the disease burden due to cardiovascular disease (CVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) is well documented in the United States [
7
–
9
]. Among all racial groups, African–Americans of all ages have the highest hypertension prevalence [
7
,
10
]. The American studies are confounded by admixture, but nonetheless, sub-Saharan African ancestry apparently plays a pivotal role in the high vulnerability of African–Americans to CVD and CKD [
11
–
13
]. Few studies compared the CVD and CKD predisposition of Blacks ‘born and living in sub-Saharan Africa’ with European Whites [
14
,
15
]. The Urinary Proteomics Combined with Home Blood Pressure Telemonitoring for Healthcare Reform Trial (UPRIGHT-HTM) is an ongoing clinical trial [
16
,
17
] with as objective to compare management of NCD risk based on telemonitoring of the home blood pressure (HTM) alone or HTM combined with risk assessment by urinary proteomic profiling (UPP). All UPRIGHT-HTM patients have to meet the same prespecified profile of traditional risk factors allowing the comparison of sub-Saharan blacks and white Europeans, even though patients were recruited in different continents.

RESULTS
Selection of patient and data
The current study includes baseline data collected up to 19 January 2024 at screening and the prerandomization visit. Figure S1 in the online only Supplementary Material shows the number of patients screened and randomized by 2-monthly time intervals. Restrictions due to the COVID19 pandemic were progressively – partially or completely – relaxed from the middle or end of 2022 onwards.
Across 16 centres, 440 patients were invited, of whom 27 did not meet the set eligibility criteria, 12 had an incompatible mobile phone, and 4 defaulted for other reasons (Fig.
1
). Of the 397 patients screened, 274 were randomized, of whom four withdrew consent and three did not adhere to HTM during the run-in period. By 18 January 2024, 116 patients were still under screening. Divergency in the timing that centres in varying geographical locations, initiated patient enrolment explains the differences in ethnic categorization, age, and anthropometrics between patients screened but not yet randomized and randomized (Table S1). Furthermore, of the 274 randomized patients, 13 Asian residents of China were excluded. Given that data collection is still ongoing and therefore incomplete, the number of patients available for the Black vs. White comparisons in the ITT analysis was 261 for traditional risk factors, 227 for ECG traits and echocardiographic left ventricular structure and function, 180 for the questionnaire data, and 165 for the urinary risk markers. Finally, of 261 randomized patients, 57 did not fully comply with all entry criteria, because they were younger than 55 years (
n
= 28), had an eGFR less than 45 ml/min/1.73 m
2
(
n
= 16), or both (
n
= 1). Sensitivity analyses according to the per-protocol approach excluded these patients.

As shown by Table S2 for common risk factors, Table S3 for the ECG and echocardiographic measurements, and Table S4 for the use of medication, the characteristics of patients randomized to control and intervention were very well balanced, suggesting that assignment to randomization group is unlikely to have had any influence on the racial and regional differences described in the following sections of the results.
Common risk factors by race
The baseline characteristics of 168 sub-Saharan blacks and 93 European whites are listed in Table
1
. The median number of risk factors (IQR), including age more than 55 years, was 8 (7–10) in Blacks and 7 (6–9) in Whites (
P
= 0.0012). Black compared to White patients, were 7.9 (SE, 0.9) years younger (60.4 vs. 68.3 years). The home and office SBPs and DBPs were similar in both racial groups with the exception of the self-measured DBP, which was 2.4 (SE, 1.1) mmHg lower in White than in Black patients (78.3 vs. 80.7 mmHg). The number of home BP readings analysed and details on their distribution are available in Table S5 and Fig. S2. As summarized in Table S6, antihypertensive drugs interfering with the renin-angiotensin system, either β-blockers (48.4 vs. 16.1%) or angiotensin-I converting-enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) or angiotensin-II receptor-I blockers (ARBs) were more frequently prescribed to White patients (86.0 vs. 70.2%), with an opposite racial trend for dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (58.3 vs. 47.3%;
P
= 0.087). Remarkably, the heart rate on home monitoring (74.5 vs. 67.5 beats per minute) as well as on office measurement (76.3 vs. 69.3 beats per minute) was faster in Blacks compared to Whites. After excluding patients taking β-blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs), the heart rate in blacks vs. whites was still higher on home monitoring (75.1 vs. 68.6 beats per minute;
P
= 0.003) as well as on office measurement (77.5 vs. 71.7 beats per minute;
P
= 0.072).

Values are mean (SD) or number of patients with condition (%). N indicates the number of patients with data within group. Home BP is the average of all available readings up to the prerandomization visit. Home hypertension is a self-measured BP of ≥135 mmHg systolic or ≥85 mmHg diastolic. Office hypertension is an office BP of ≥40 mmHg systolic or ≥90 mmHg diastolic. If SBP and DBP were in different categories, patients were classified in the highest category. White-coat hypertension is an elevated office BP combined with a normal home BP. Masked hypertension is a normal office BP combined with an elevated home BP pressure. Sustained hypertension is hypertension on home and office measurement. Home and office BP are cross-classified irrespective of antihypertensive drug treatment. Diabetes is a diagnosis provided by the caregiver and documented in local medical records. Treated diabetes refers to patients on antidiabetic drugs. Current smoking was inhaling tobacco smoke on a daily basis. Drinking alcohol was the occasional or daily consumption of ethanol containing beverages. Physical inactivity is engaging in less than 150 min of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (3–6 METS) throughout the week.

DISCUSSION
The current study involved baseline data from an ongoing clinical trial and involved Blacks, born and living in sub-Saharan countries, and European Whites enrolled in Belgium, Poland, and Slovenia. All patients had to comply with the same eligibility criteria and had to be at a high risk for CVD, CKD, or both. Black patients had a median of eight risk factors and white patients seven. Being younger (60.4 vs. 68.3 years), Blacks had a worse risk profile, as evidenced by higher diabetes prevalence, higher BMI, faster heart rate, unfavourable serum cholesterol fractions, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate, microalbuminuria, and sedentary lifestyle. This resulted in Blacks having higher 10-year CVD risk, higher heart age (index of vascular ageing with chronological age as reference), and a worse CKD grades. In both races, CKD273 increased with CKD grade, but CKD273 and HF1 were not different by race. These observations were robust in subgroup and adjusted analyses.
A remarkable finding, which was not abolished by adjustment of the more frequent use of β-blockers in Europeans, was the higher heart rate in Blacks than Whites, both on home monitoring and at the office. The average annual temperature is likely to explain this observation, which is 5°C–9°C range for Poland, 12°C for Mediterranean Slovenia, but 26.9°C in the whole of Nigeria and around 23°C in the Potchefstroom area in South Africa (World Meteorological Organization). Over the year, the climate is more than 10°C warmer in the sub-Saharan than the European catchment area of UPRIGHT-HTM patients. In an experimental setting, 37 older adults (61–80 years) rested for 8 h in 31 and 36°C (45% relative humidity) [
23
]. Diabetes was the predictor of the end-exposure heart rate (with vs. without, 13 beats per minute; 95% CI, 6–23). In the present study, the prevalence of diabetes was 49.4 vs. 26.9 in Black compared to White patients. Exposure to high temperature also leads to stimulation of the sympathetic system and parasympathetic tone withdrawal [
24
]. In 274 randomly recruited Flemish (50% women; mean age, 40.6 years), the odds of endothelial dysfunction, as assessed by the flow-mediated vasodilatation in the brachial artery, increased by 58% (95% CI, 4–141;
P
= 0.03) for each 10°C increment in the ambient daily temperature averaged over 1 week [
25
].
The FRS was developed and frequently applied in Whites [
22
,
26
], but was further validated in African–American [
27
,
28
]. The Jackson Heart Study [
28
] included 3689 Black adults (averaged 53 years, 64.8% women), among whom 270 participants experienced a first CVD event during the 9.1-year follow-up. The FRS proved to be effective in prediction risk in black individuals with only marginal improvement of risk assessment by other risk factors, such as B-type natriuretic peptide or the ankle-brachial index [
28
]. Moreover, the FRS was further validated in a multiethnic study (
n
= 23,424) comprising six prospectively followed US cohorts, including Whites, African–Americans, American Japanese, and Hispanics, indicating reliable performance after recalibration [
27
]. In accordance with our study, American Blacks had a higher CVD risk profile, including higher BMI, serum uric acid, SBP, and prevalence of habitual smoking compared to American Whites [
29
]. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also highlighted the higher cardiovascular disease prevalence in Blacks than Whites with a Black-White prevalence ratio of 1.9 (95% CI, 1.1–3.4) in young adulthood (35–44 years), which decreased with advancing age (
P
= 0.04). Modifiable social and environmental risk factors play an important role in the racial disparity to CVD and CKD, not only in the US, but also sub-Saharan Africa [
30
].
Study limitations
What sets this study apart is the involvement of Blacks born and living in sub-Saharan Africa, and European Whites. While genetic admixture cannot be excluded in South African Blacks, presumably, it is less of a confounding factor compared with studies conducted in the United States [
7
–
10
]. The same eligibility criteria were applicable in Africa and Europe to screen and randomise patients. Nevertheless, the present study must be interpreted within the context of several limitations. First and foremost, this study did not differentiate host factors, which could be genetic or downstream pathogenic molecular pathways, from environmental drivers of ill health, such living in widely different climate zones, exposure to pollutants, parasitic and infectious agents, such as Anopheles mosquitos or HIV, and an unhealthy lifestyle with physical inactivity or a shifting preference of Black individuals for Westernised diets rich in refined sugars, fat and processed foods. Second, of 261 randomized patients, 57 did not fully comply with all entry criteria, because they were younger than 55 years (
n
= 28), had an eGFR less than 45 ml/min/1.73 m
2
(
n
= 16), or both (
n
= 1). This was to be expected in a trial running in so diverse regions and varying internet access. Therefore, the protocol pro-actively included the provision of an ITT and per-protocol analysis. Both produced similar results in this preliminary analysis. As UPRIGHT-HTM is ongoing, a larger sample size will be attained at the later stage of our study. Third, not all the black and white participants had UPP measurement. Therefore, we did not have enough power to explain the lower HF1 levels in Blacks than Whites. Finally, Asian participants were excluded from the current analysis, as there were few in number, giving that recruitment for UPRIGHT-HTM is still ongoing.
A call to action
To address the NCD burden, driven by hypertension, diabetes, and health problems related to climate change and environmental degradation, a framework shift is necessary in sub-Saharan countries to deliver better health outcomes through people-centred health systems, with focuses on prevention, primary care, and public health [
1
]. Countries should invest more in health and do more to address inefficiencies by identification of new funding sources and movement towards prioritization of health in domestic budgets [
1
]. Furthermore, an analysis of the Food and Agricultural Organization database and health indicators supplied by UNICEF and WHO revealed different dietary patterns in sub-Saharan Africa: a Westernized diet with high content of refined sugars, sweeteners, alcohol, meat, animal fats, eggs, and dairy in South Africa, and a high consumption of cereals, nuts, fish and vegetable oils in Nigeria, particularly in coastal areas [
31
]. The median values of health indicators explained the high prevalence of NCD in South Africa, where stunting and anaemia are higher than in other sub-Saharan regions [
31
]. The EAT Lancet Commission proposed that healthy diets should have an appropriate caloric intake and consist of a diversity of plant-based foods, low amounts of animal source foods, unsaturated rather than saturated fats, and small amounts of refined grains, highly processed foods, and added sugars [
6
].
About 40% of Nigerians live in poverty, in social conditions that create ill health, and with the ever-present risk of catastrophic expenditures from high out-of-pocket spending for health. Even compared with countries of similar income levels in Africa, Nigeria's population health outcomes are poor, with national statistics masking drastic differences between rich and poor, urban and rural populations, and different regions [
2
]. The Lancet
Nigeria
Commission, in line with the mission statement of the Alliance for the Promotion of Preventive Medicine (
www.appremed.org
), prevention should be at the heart of health policies, given Nigeria's young population. To achieve this goal will require lifecourse approach to disease prevention [
32
] and the unwavering engagement to invest in prevention by the Nigerian federal and regional authorities and the community as a whole [
2
]. An explicit consideration of equity in the implementation of programmes and provision of social welfare, education, and employment opportunities should be paramount [
2
].
Investment in higher education and research is essential for better health and sustainable development by enhancing research capacity for identification of challenges and devising local solutions. The International Society of Hypertension (ISH [
https://ish-world.com/about-ish
]) is committed to scientific innovation in the field of hypertension and in a wider context in addressing the risk factors underlying CVD and CKD. ISH also endorses the international exchange and promotion of investigators, teachers, and students, the advocation of patient right, and the education of the public as well as medical professionals. Along with other national and international learned societies and in collaboration with regional health professionals, ISH is geared to take up its role in promoting health in sub-Saharan Africa.
CONCLUSION
In contrast to Whites in living Europe, Blacks born and living in sub-Saharan Africa had a higher risk profile of CVD and CKD, as by their risk factors load, the FRS, heart age, and their worse distribution across the KDIGO CKD grades. This study did not differentiate host (genetic, molecular, and pathogenic) from environmental drivers of disease. Nonetheless, the findings call for a multipronged and comprehensive implementation of innovative health policies in sub-Saharan countries. Education, research, empowerment of stakeholders, and international learned societies connecting experts from a wide array of disciplines should vigorously sustain this effort.
